models.collectorNote: Hemi 'Cuda convertibles sit at the very top of the muscle market; documented 440 cars follow. Clones are everywhere — fender tags and build sheets are non-negotiable homework.

generations.name: Barracuda (first generation)
generations.note: A fastback A-body with a 7-foot fold-down rear compartment. Formula S cars added handling and the 273 V8 — the pony formula, from Plymouth, first.

generations.name: 'Cuda (E-body)
generations.note: Big-block 440s, the 440+6, and the 426 Hemi at 425 hp. The AAR 'Cuda's 340 and side pipes chased Trans-Am glory; Hemi convertibles — 14 built across 1970–71 — became the most valuable muscle cars of all.

models.intro: Launched April 1, 1964 — two weeks before the Mustang — on Valiant bones with the biggest rear window in the business. By 1970 the E-body 'Cuda had become the muscle era's apex predator, and the Hemi convertible its holy grail.
models.name: Barracuda

models.collectorNote: Hemi and Six Barrel cars lead; Superbirds are their own market entirely. The beep-beep horn and cartoon decals must be original-spec — the details are the car.

generations.name: Road Runner (first era)
generations.note: 383 standard, 440 Six Barrel added 1969, 426 Hemi optional throughout. The Superbird (1970) was built to lure Richard Petty back — about 1,900 road cars satisfied NASCAR's homologation.

models.intro: Plymouth paid Warner Bros. for the cartoon bird and spent the savings on speed: a stripped B-body, a 383 with magnum internals, and a 'meep meep' horn. The 1970 Superbird wore a nose cone and a wing for NASCAR — and for immortality.
models.name: Road Runner

generations.name: GTX
generations.note: 440 power at 375 hp for most; the 1967 cars are the sleeper pick, the 1971 the last of the line as compression and insurance closed in.

models.intro: The gentleman's muscle car: Plymouth's upscale B-body with the 440 Super Commando standard and the Hemi on the option list, pitched at buyers who wanted the pace without the stripper spec.
models.name: GTX

models.collectorNote: 340 cars are the appreciating ones; slant-six cars are the charming ones. Feather Dusters — aluminium panels from the fuel-crisis years — are the trivia-night rarity.

generations.name: Duster 340
generations.note: The 340's 275 hp in a light A-body was the budget performance equation of the early seventies. Later cars softened into economy trim as the era ended.

models.intro: The budget bruiser: a Valiant fastback coupe that, with the 340 small-block, outran cars twice its price and embarrassed its own stablemates. The Twister trim sold the look; the 340 sold the legend.
models.name: Duster

models.collectorNote: Limited editions and the trailer option (yes, a matching trailer) amuse collectors. Values are stable-niche: buy the colour you want — purple and yellow lead the room.

generations.name: Prowler
generations.note: The 3.5 V6 rose from 214 to 253 hp with the 1999 aluminium-block update. About 11,700 were built including the Chrysler-badged final cars after Plymouth closed.

models.intro: A factory hot rod in 1997: aluminium-intensive, open-wheeled retro styling, and a concept car Chrysler actually built. The V6-only powertrain was the compromise; the look was not.
models.name: Prowler

models.collectorNote: Survivors are scarce — they were used up, as intended. Turbo five-speed cars are the unicorns; condition and nostalgia, not spec, drive the tiny market.

generations.name: Voyager (first generation)
generations.note: Four-cylinder, turbo-four, or Mitsubishi V6 power — modest, but the package was the revolution. The turbo vans are the sleeper trivia answer; the woody Grand Voyager is the period piece.

models.intro: With the Dodge Caravan, the 1984 Voyager invented the modern minivan: front-wheel drive, a car floor height, and a sliding door, selling families out of station wagons by the millions. Lee Iacocca's second act saved Chrysler.
models.name: Voyager
